Cross-file taint [direct, sink]: service_exchange() in auth.py reaches a sink via verify_service_token() from security.py. A JWT/bearer token is decoded or verified (PyJWT/python-jose's
`jwt.decode(...)`, jsonwebtoken's `jwt.verify(...)`, or jose's
`jwtVerify(...)`) with no `audience` check anywhere nearby. RFC 8707
(Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0), which the MCP authorization spec
requires, exists specifically because a token's SIGNATURE validating
does not prove it was issued FOR this server -- an authorization
server that also issues tokens for other resources will happily sign
a token whose `aud` claim names a different service entirely. A
server that verifies the signature but not the audience will accept
any validly-signed token from that authorization server, regardless
of which resource it was actually issued for -- the confused-deputy
mechanism behind the class `TNT-ML-025` only catches when the token
is visibly forwarded in-function; this catches it even when the token
never leaves the function that decoded it, because the flaw is in
the decode itself.
Engine limitation: presence + absence-in-window, like every other
NeuroScan rule -- an `audience=`/`audience:` check that validates the
WRONG value (a client ID instead of the resource identifier, or a
value read from the token itself) still suppresses this finding.
Triage against what the audience is actually compared to.
Open redirect: user-controlled URL in redirect.

A credential-shaped URL query parameter (token/access_token/api_key/...) is read directly from the query string. Query strings are logged by web servers and proxies, sent to third-party origins via the Referer header on any outbound request the page makes, and persist in browser history -- all leak the credential outside the TLS-protected request body. Accept the same credential via the Authorization header (or a POST body) instead.

Web application debug / development mode is enabled (CWE-215). A running server with debug on exposes interactive stack traces, source snippets, config, and (Werkzeug/Flask) an evaluable console: remote code and full config disclosure. This fires on the debug flag being turned ON in code: Flask app.run(debug=True) / app.debug=True / app.config["DEBUG"]=True, Django DEBUG=True, FastAPI/Starlette/Tornado(debug=True), and DEBUG read from an environment variable with a TRUTHY default (a fail-open default that ships debug on unless the environment overrides it). Set debug off in production and make any env-var default fail closed (default False / "0").

Regex contains a nested quantifier -- a quantified group whose entire content is itself a single quantified atom (e.g. `(a+)+`, `([a-z0-9]+ )*`, `(\d*)+`), or a repeated group with two identical alternation branches (e.g. `(a|a)*`). Both shapes admit exponentially many ways to partition a matching prefix across the outer repetition, so a catastrophic-backtracking (ReDoS) input can make a single match call take seconds to hours. If this pattern is ever matched against request-derived input (a form field, header, or query parameter), one request can pin a worker thread.
Broken authorization lets ordinary authenticated users control server-authored MCP tool description metadata.

MCP tool description is not a fixed string literal -- it is a bare
variable/attribute reference, a function/method call result, or an
f-string that interpolates a non-literal expression. The tool
description is injected verbatim into the client model's own context
window on every session; if the description can change after the
user approved the tool (fetched from a registry/config at import or
call time, computed from mutable state) the change is invisible to
the user and becomes an instruction-injection channel the user never
re-reviewed (Invariant Labs 2025 tool-poisoning / "rug pull"
disclosure). Presence signal only: a reference to a module-level
string constant would also match this heuristic; if the referenced
value is fixed at import time and never reassigned or fetched
remotely, this is a false positive -- inline it as a literal to
silence the finding, or confirm the value truly is static. Distinct
from NS-AIML-009 (which flags any exposed MCP tool regardless of its
description) and ns-aiml-066 (tool-call-smuggling on mcp.run/serve);
this rule is specifically about the description field as an
injection channel.

Scoped to a same-line tool-constructor/decorator call (Tool(,
FunctionTool(, StructuredTool(, BaseTool(, @mcp.tool(, @server.tool(,
@app.tool() -- a bare `description=` kwarg is far too common a name
(Pydantic model fields, argparse, unrelated dataclasses) to use as a
standalone signal, and this regex engine can't verify multi-line call
membership. This trades recall on multi-line constructor calls
(`description=` on its own line inside a call opened elsewhere) for
eliminating the flood of unrelated `description=` kwargs this rule
matched before the same-line anchor was added.

A cookie is set without an `httponly` argument. Flask, Django, and Starlette/FastAPI all default it to False, so the value is readable from JavaScript via `document.cookie` -- any XSS anywhere on the origin can exfiltrate it. If this cookie carries a session or auth token, that turns a contained XSS into full account takeover.

A cookie is set without the `secure` flag (or with `secure=False`). Flask, Django, and Starlette/FastAPI all default it to False, so the browser will send this cookie over plain HTTP -- a network attacker on the path (public Wi-Fi, a downgraded link, a captive portal) reads it directly. If it carries a session or auth token, that is session hijacking with no XSS required. Pass `secure=True` on any cookie that authenticates the request.

A container is created through the Docker SDK with none of the options
that would actually isolate it. With no network_mode the container joins
the default bridge and has full outbound network access; with no user it
runs as whatever the image's default is, usually root; with no cap_drop
or security_opt it keeps the default capability set; with no mem_limit or
pids_limit it can exhaust the host.

This matters most when the container is the sandbox for untrusted or
model-generated code. A bind-mounted host directory is then writable by
that code, which turns "run this snippet in a container" into a host file
write, and full egress turns it into an exfiltration and SSRF path to the
cloud metadata service.

Any one isolation option present in the surrounding lines suppresses this
finding, on the assumption that an author who set one considered the
others. The rule flags the case where none was set at all.

Docker container with privileged mode or host socket mount.
Grants full host access. Use capability-based security (--cap-add) instead.

A value chosen by the model (an LLM completion, a parsed structured output, or a tool-call argument) reaches the owner/tenant/principal argument of a database read. The query looks correctly scoped, but the identity it scopes to is attacker-influenceable: anything that can steer the model -- a prompt injection in retrieved content, a poisoned tool description, a crafted user message -- can redirect the read at another user's rows. The principal must come from the session (request.user, current_user), never from the model. Suppressed when the claimed identity is compared against the server-side principal, or passed to an authorization decision, in a guard that exits before the query (see guard_clause.py's "principal" shape).

A guardrail's result is bound and tested in a conditional, but no path out of that branch terminates the request -- the branch only logs, increments a metric, or falls through, and execution continues to the model call. The verdict is observed and then ignored, which reads as enforcement in review while behaving identically to having no guardrail. Engine limitation: only single-target assignments are matched. A guard whose API returns a tuple (`sanitized, results, score = scan_prompt(q)`, LLM Guard's documented shape) is a known residual gap.

A multi-agent orchestration construct (AutoGen `GroupChat`, LangGraph
`StateGraph`, or CrewAI `Crew`) with no visible turn/round/iteration
cap (`max_round`, `recursion_limit`, `max_iter`, `max_turns`) anywhere
nearby. Issue #188 (epic #183): related to `ns-aiml-120`'s unbounded
`while True` around a single completion call, but structurally
different -- the loop here lives in the DELEGATION GRAPH (agent A
hands off to B, which hands back to A, ...), not in ordinary control
flow, so `ns-aiml-120` cannot see it. A cyclic or open-ended handoff
topology with no cap means a misbehaving or adversarially-steered
agent can keep the delegation loop running indefinitely, exhausting
the token/rate budget the same way an unbounded reflection loop does.
Engine limitation: presence + absence-in-window, like every other
NeuroScan rule here -- this cannot verify the topology is actually
cyclic (a genuinely acyclic, one-pass handoff chain with no natural
termination condition looks identical to this rule), so it is a
cycle-agnostic "unbounded orchestration session" signal, not a
confirmed-cyclic-graph one. Triage against the actual handoff graph.

A container is run (or defined via docker-compose) with `privileged=True`
/ `privileged: true`, a `/var/run/docker.sock` bind mount, `network_mode`/
`pid_mode` set to `"host"`, or `SYS_ADMIN` added to its capabilities. Any
one of these is a documented container-escape primitive on its own --
mounting the Docker socket into a container an LLM-driven agent can
reach gives it the ability to launch new, arbitrary containers on the
HOST engine (full host takeover, not merely "escape this one
container"), and this exact shape is a common tutorial pattern for
giving an agent a "code execution sandbox." `pid_mode`/`network_mode:
host` similarly erase the isolation a container is supposed to provide.
Issue #189 (epic #183).

Dynamic code execution is handed an explicit globals mapping that
defines __builtins__ as a dict of "safe" names. A __builtins__ dict is
not a sandbox. Any executed string reaches the full interpreter in
four lines through the object graph, for example
().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__() to find BuiltinImporter and
import anything, without ever touching the __import__ entry that was
so carefully replaced. LMCache shipped exactly this shape behind an
unauthenticated /run_script endpoint, which is unauthenticated RCE.
There is no allowlist of builtins, no name filter and no AST check
that makes this safe, so do not tune the dict: remove the dynamic
execution endpoint, or move execution into a real OS-level sandbox
(separate process, seccomp/gVisor/container, no host filesystem or
network) and authenticate and authorise the caller.

An agent tool (or a bare `os.system`/`subprocess` call reachable from
one) executes shell commands or arbitrary code with no recognized
sandbox mechanism (E2B, Modal, Daytona, Docker, gVisor, nsjail,
Firecracker, RestrictedPython/`compile_restricted`, Pyodide) visible
anywhere nearby. This is the confirmatory escalation of
`NS-AIML-010`/`NS-AIML-011` (which flag the dangerous call as a bare
presence signal regardless of context): when nothing that looks like a
sandbox appears in the surrounding code at all, this is no longer "an
agent has a shell tool" but "an agent has direct, unsandboxed host
access." Issue #189 (epic #183).
Engine limitation: presence + absence-in-window, like every other
NeuroScan rule -- a sandbox implemented in a different file this rule
doesn't scan (a separate sandboxing service the tool calls out to)
will still be flagged; triage against the actual execution path. This
necessarily co-fires with `NS-AIML-010`/`011` on the same line by
design (see the fix note there) -- it is a stronger, escalated signal
layered on the same evidence, not an accidental duplicate rule (DEF-10
is about byte-identical patterns meant to be one rule; this is a
deliberately distinct, complementary check).

A completion API call (.chat.completions.create/.completions.create/
.messages.create/openai.ChatCompletion.create/openai.Completion.create/
litellm.completion/litellm.acompletion/.text_generation) with no
max_tokens, max_completion_tokens, or max_new_tokens argument within 10
lines. Provider defaults, where a cap is optional, can be the model's
own maximum context/output length -- combined with no rate limiting,
each request can cost as much as the model allows. This is a
heuristic INFO-level surface signal, not a confirmed vulnerability:
the regex engine cannot verify this call site is a request/route
handler specifically (that structural recognition -- GitHub issue
#122's cross_file.py AST pass -- is not reachable from a regex-mode
rule), so it fires on every completion call missing the kwarg,
including intentionally-unbounded offline/batch scripts. Triage
accordingly; low confidence by design (see the low-confidence INFO
convention other ns-aiml-* rules use).

A JWT/bearer token is decoded or verified (PyJWT/python-jose's
`jwt.decode(...)`, jsonwebtoken's `jwt.verify(...)`, or jose's
`jwtVerify(...)`) with no `audience` check anywhere nearby. RFC 8707
(Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0), which the MCP authorization spec
requires, exists specifically because a token's SIGNATURE validating
does not prove it was issued FOR this server -- an authorization
server that also issues tokens for other resources will happily sign
a token whose `aud` claim names a different service entirely. A
server that verifies the signature but not the audience will accept
any validly-signed token from that authorization server, regardless
of which resource it was actually issued for -- the confused-deputy
mechanism behind the class `TNT-ML-025` only catches when the token
is visibly forwarded in-function; this catches it even when the token
never leaves the function that decoded it, because the flaw is in
the decode itself.
Engine limitation: presence + absence-in-window, like every other
NeuroScan rule -- an `audience=`/`audience:` check that validates the
WRONG value (a client ID instead of the resource identifier, or a
value read from the token itself) still suppresses this finding.
Triage against what the audience is actually compared to.

Inference/serving code constructs a plain jinja2.Environment (or a
get_jinja_env-style factory) instead of a SandboxedEnvironment. This is
the structural half of the SGLang CVE-2026-5760 class (also
CVE-2025-61620 vLLM, CVE-2024-34359 "Llama Drama"): a non-sandboxed Jinja
env that renders any attacker-publishable model-metadata field
(chat_template, tokenizer/generation/adapter config) is SSTI -> RCE.
Presence signal, WARNING: the real dataflow detection is TNT-ML-028
(rules/ml_taint.yaml), which confirms a model-metadata read actually
reaches the render. Intended scope is serving/inference files (vllm,
sglang, transformers, text_generation); the line-by-line regex engine
cannot require a co-occurring framework import on a separate line (no
file-level AND in NeuroScanRule.check), so precision comes structurally
from matching only explicit non-sandboxed Environment CONSTRUCTION, which
an ordinary Flask/Django app using render_template does not do. A web app
that hand-builds its own unsandboxed jinja2.Environment is still flagged,
which is itself the risky shape. Sibling to TNT-ML-028; seeing both is
expected, not duplicate reporting.

Jinja2 Environment(autoescape=False) renders template variables without
HTML escaping -- user-controlled content becomes a stored-XSS sink.
Enable autoescape=True or escape untrusted values explicitly.

A `while True:`/`while 1:` loop with no iteration-cap term (
max_iterations/max_turns/max_steps/max_loops/recursion_limit/
iteration_limit/MAX_ITER/deadline/time.time()/time.monotonic()) within
10 lines. Agent "reflection" loops that call a completion API and
rely on the MODEL's own output to decide when to stop (e.g. `if "DONE"
in reply: break`) are still unbounded from a cost/availability
standpoint -- termination must be CODE-controlled (a counter compared
against a fixed limit, or a wall-clock deadline), not model-decided,
or a misbehaving/adversarially-steered model can loop indefinitely
and exhaust the token/rate budget (Sourcegraph Cody and multiple
OpenAI-bill-runaway postmortems are this exact loop-amplification
shape). Engine limitation: this regex-based signal cannot verify a
completion API call is actually inside the loop body, or that a
`break` statement it does find is code-controlled rather than
model-controlled -- it only checks for the ABSENCE of a recognized
cap term nearby. Triage against the loop body; a `while True:` with no
completion call at all is a false positive for this specific concern.

An agent tool (or a bare `os.system`/`subprocess` call reachable from
one) executes shell commands or arbitrary code with no recognized
sandbox mechanism (E2B, Modal, Daytona, Docker, gVisor, nsjail,
Firecracker, RestrictedPython/`compile_restricted`, Pyodide) visible
anywhere nearby. This is the confirmatory escalation of
`NS-AIML-010`/`NS-AIML-011` (which flag the dangerous call as a bare
presence signal regardless of context): when nothing that looks like a
sandbox appears in the surrounding code at all, this is no longer "an
agent has a shell tool" but "an agent has direct, unsandboxed host
access." Issue #189 (epic #183).
Engine limitation: presence + absence-in-window, like every other
NeuroScan rule -- a sandbox implemented in a different file this rule
doesn't scan (a separate sandboxing service the tool calls out to)
will still be flagged; triage against the actual execution path. This
necessarily co-fires with `NS-AIML-010`/`011` on the same line by
design (see the fix note there) -- it is a stronger, escalated signal
layered on the same evidence, not an accidental duplicate rule (DEF-10
is about byte-identical patterns meant to be one rule; this is a
deliberately distinct, complementary check).
